title: Contorting Giants
caption: The lensed galaxy LRG-3-817, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, S. Allam et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A long arc curves to the left of a central cluster of galaxies in this Hubble picture. The arc is the galaxy LRG-3-817 (cataloged too as SDSS J090122.37+181432.3), and its image has been stretched by gravitational lensing.

Lensing happens when a large mass, a galaxy cluster for instance, lies between us and a far-off light source. Massive objects warp space, so light from the far object bends on its way to us and arrives as a distorted image. Einstein's general theory of relativity first predicted the effect.

Strong lenses are useful because Hubble can pick out details inside the arcs they create. Lensing also magnifies, bringing into view objects too distant and too dim to detect otherwise. Hubble uses that boost to study objects beyond the reach of its 2.4-meter main mirror, including the most distant galaxies ever seen.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this field in visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Some of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the lensed arc is far too faint for any unaided eye.

explore: LRG-3-817 was found by the Sloan Bright Arcs Survey, which turned up some of the brightest lensed high-redshift galaxies in the night sky. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded the field through filters from blue-green visible light to the near-infrared.
alt: A galaxy cluster with a long, curved arc of light to the left of center.
